results.title: Should you build an agent for your design system
results.content:
An agent that automatically pushes token changes to production across 12 codebases? Extremely high risk. One wrong semantic mapping, and your entire product suite has the wrong error colors. Keep this read-only, with human approval gates at every step.

5. Can you trust the output?

There’s a design systems angle to agents that almost nobody is discussing yet. Design systems are trust infrastructure.

Teams adopt your tokens, components, and patterns because they produce consistent, predictable results every time. Agents introduce variability. Run the same prompt twice, and you might get two different outputs. That’s fine for a blog draft. It’s a problem when the agent is deciding which semantic token maps `color.background.danger` across your component library. [...] ### Token validation → Workflow

The rules are static. You know exactly what correct looks like. Check if raw hex values are used instead of tokens, flag primitives used directly in components. AST parsing and token matching are solved problems. Each individual check is cheap, and false positives are just noise.

Write a linter. Run it in CI. Done.

### Component documentation generation → Agent with human review

This one gets interesting. Reading code, extracting props, understanding usage patterns, writing clear descriptions. There’s real judgment involved. And documentation is the #1 complaint about every design system, so the payoff is high. [...] 2. Is the task valuable enough?

If each task run saves less than $0.10 of human time, use a workflow. If it saves more than $1.00 per run, an agent starts making economic sense.

Checking a file for unused imports? Pennies. Not worth an agent.

Migrating 200 components from one token schema to another, where each component needs contextual decisions about which new token maps to the old one? That’s hours of human work per component. An agent pays for itself on the first run.

3. Are all parts of the task doable?

results.title: Medium
results.content:
The craft of design systems — the systems thinking, the stakeholder work, the iteration discipline — stays with the designer. What the agent removes is the blank-page problem. You start from something real, and you take it somewhere.

## Try It

The Design System Agent is live inside Claude. Give it a real brief — something you’re actually building, or a project you’ve been thinking about. See what it generates, push on the edges, tell me where it breaks.

I built this because I think the most underserved users of design systems tooling aren’t the enterprise teams with dedicated platform designers. They’re the people moving fast, building something real, with no time to do this “properly” — and who deserve a principled foundation anyway. [...] I’ve spent years designing AI platform experiences for products that sit at the intersection of complex systems, advanced tooling, and human judgment. What struck me, over and over, was how the teams with the least capacity were making the most expensive design decisions: not because they were careless, but because they had no viable on-ramp.

So I built one.

The Design System Agent is not a tool for building a sophisticated, production-grade design system. It’s a tool for having something real on day 1 — principled starting point that reflects how good design systems actually work, generated from three inputs in under a minute.

## Who This Is For

I had two personas in mind throughout the entire build. Every structural decision traces back to them. [...] This distinction shaped everything.

The 2-tier token architecture exists because conflating brand tokens with semantic tokens is where most improvised design systems break down. Teams end up with a variable called `--blue` that's used for both the primary action colour and the info state, and changing one breaks the other. The agent separates these from the start: Tier 1 is your brand identity (primary colour, typeface, border radius, shadow) — flexible by design. Tier 2 is your semantic system (spacing scale, type scale, status colours) — structured, with guardrails. When you grow the system, you're adding to a hierarchy, not untangling a flat list.
